issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Similar cars' is hard to reconcile as a salient trigger unless there is a very specific undisclosed trauma context; it reads as a transport/accident-associated cue rather than illness-related.

'Related people/known people' can occur around illness trauma, but paired with other selected triggers and threat items it suggests an interpersonal or assault-like threat context more than a medical illness context.

Scanning for exits is much more characteristic of fear of external attack or entrapment than of trauma centered on life-threatening illness, and is difficult to connect coherently to the rest of an illness-based profile.
Reacting to unexpected nearby movement as if in danger is also more typical of assault/combat-type threat expectations than illness trauma, creating a mismatch with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Being Praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless paired with illness-specific meanings elsewhere (e.g., praise for surviving, coping, or returning to function). No corresponding appraisal or memory content makes this trigger clinically coherent here.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Scanning Exits' and 'Startle to Movement' imply a danger formulation centered on assault/attack or external interpersonal threat, which is difficult to reconcile with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you' similarly reflects fear of intentional human harm rather than recurrence of illness, bodily catastrophe, medical procedures, or death from disease. This is poorly aligned with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Going Out' would be coherent if linked to infection fears, collapse in public, or medical reminders, but those meanings are not represented in the trigger, threat, or appraisal items selected. As written, it appears to address a different threat context than the rest of the profile.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'related people' as a trigger is plausible, but the profile otherwise anchors triggers strongly in medical reminders and bodily danger rather than interpersonal threat. This item becomes hard to reconcile because the accompanying appraisal and threat items do not explain why known people specifically function as a major trigger.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' implies an interpersonal perpetrator-based worldview. That is difficult to align with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness, especially when the rest of the profile centers medical cues, sleep disturbance, startle, and physical reactivity rather than harm from other people. A more illness- or vulnerability-focused appraisal would fit better.

For a life-threatening illness trauma, medical triggers like needles, drips, and procedures are coherent, but alcohol smell is not plausibly linked to the trauma context unless there is additional undisclosed treatment context; it stands out as a hard-to-explain trigger relative to the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a 19-year-old male with life-threatening illness trauma. The other appraisals center on bodily vulnerability and loss of meaning, whereas a failed core-role appraisal implies a specific disrupted identity or responsibility that is otherwise absent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out
issues.explanation: Avoiding going out is weakly connected to the rest of the selected items. The profile is dominated by medical reminders and internal threat/bodily vulnerability, so broad avoidance of leaving home lacks a clear clinical target here and is not well explained by the trigger-threat-appraisal pattern shown.

vignette:
Daniel was 19, a European American college student who worked part-time as a counselor at a youth drop-in centre, and he described his life as having split cleanly into before and after the illness. The change began the winter he was rushed to hospital with a sudden, life-threatening infection that left him attached to drips, surrounded by beeping monitors, and repeatedly examined by staff in blue gloves under the sharp smell of antiseptic. He remembered the cold of the examination room, the sight of needles and tubing in his arm, and the helplessness of being told what was happening to his body while he felt it slipping out of his control. Even now, walking past a clinic entrance or catching that hospital smell in a pharmacy or at work, he would feel the moment snap back with alarming force. The equipment itself had become charged with danger for him: a needle, a drip stand, the snap of a glove, even a nearby ambulance siren on the street outside the centre where he worked could pull him straight back to that bed. Those cues did more than unsettle him; they made him physically tense, his heart racing and his body jolting as if danger were right in front of him, and they left him convinced that his body was not something he could trust anymore.

In the weeks after discharge, Daniel began arranging his life around those reactions. He avoided hospitals and any medical examination whenever he could, found excuses not to look at therapy material if it touched on the illness, and developed the habit of staying up until very late so he would not have to face sleep and the thoughts that came with it. He told himself that if he kept busy at the drop-in centre and never let his mind settle, he could keep the memories from surfacing. But the more he tried to push away reminders, the more alert he became to them. He would scan corridors for the smell of antiseptic, stiffen at the movement of a staff member passing behind him, and react to any unexpected motion nearby as if he were about to be hurt. Sleep became unreliable too, with trouble both falling asleep and staying asleep, and the fatigue made him even more jumpy the next day. At work, if a young person mentioned blood tests or an ambulance, he felt the familiar surge in his chest and would quickly change the subject or step out of the room, telling himself he could not afford to be caught off guard.

As those reactions repeated, Daniel’s thoughts about himself and his future darkened. He had come to believe that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, because everything he had assumed about strength and health had been taken away so abruptly. He no longer trusted his own body; it seemed to him that it kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe, and that made every sensation feel suspicious. A skipped heartbeat, a wave of nausea, or a sudden flush of heat could become proof, in his mind, that illness was returning. That belief made medical cues feel even more potent. The sight of a needle in a tray, the press of a blood-pressure cuff, or the smell of a hospital corridor did not merely remind him of what happened; they now seemed to announce that his body was fragile and that he might be sliding back toward the same terrifying loss of control. In turn, that sharpened his urge to stay away from anything medical, to avoid therapy content that might bring the illness into focus, and to put off sleep until exhaustion finally took him under.

The more Daniel organized his days around avoiding those reminders, the more threatened he felt. Staying up late left him depleted and more reactive to small movements and sudden noises; lack of rest made his startle response worse, and the stronger his physical reactions became, the more convinced he was that something was wrong with him. He noticed that even in ordinary settings—at the youth centre, on public transport, or in a waiting room for his partner’s appointment—his body seemed to brace for impact. That constant alertness made the original hospital cues seem even harder to escape, because once he was already keyed up, the smell of antiseptic or the sight of medical equipment could hit him with overwhelming force. He found himself narrowing his world further, ducking out of conversations, avoiding anything that might touch on treatment or illness, and feeling ashamed that as a counselor he could help others sit with distress yet could not bear his own memories. By the time he came for help, Daniel was frightened by how small his life had become and how certain he was that his body would betray him again. What brought him in was the fear that he could not keep living in this tense, sleepless state, and what he hoped for—though he scarcely trusted it was possible—was to feel safe in his own body again and to find some meaning in a life that no longer felt like his.
